title: Not-self, taught
hookLine: to the five: is the body you, is feeling, is any of the five heaps mine (SN 22.59)

lines: WHO ARE YOU, IN ONE SENTENCE?
cards: Who are you, in one sentence? The answers tend to reach for the same things. My body.
My job. My feelings about things. My memories, my opinions, my personality.
That's me. A few days after the first sermon, all five companions have understood the basics, and the Buddha sits them down in the Deer Park again. This time he goes after that one sentence.
He takes the pieces you point to when you say me, holds each one up to the light, and asks a very simple question about it. It's the second teaching in the old accounts.

teach.b: Not-self. In Pali, anatta. The teaching is called the Discourse on the Characteristic of Not-self, and it works like a careful conversation.

First the Buddha names five heaps, the bundles that make up a person as you experience one: the body; feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither; perception, recognizing things; mental formations, urges and habits; and consciousness, the knowing.
Then he asks about the body. If the body were really your self, it wouldn't lead to trouble, and you could just say: let my body be like this, not like that. But you can't.
It gets sick. It ages. It doesn't take orders.

teach.h: IS IT PERMANENT? IS IT MINE?
teach.b: Is the body permanent or impermanent, he asks. Impermanent, they say. And is something impermanent a source of lasting ease, or of unease?
Unease. Then is it right to look at it and say, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, they say.
He asks the same of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Same answers every time. The texts say that as the five heard this, their minds were freed.
Two things are worth knowing. First, it's a practice more than a philosophy: you look at a feeling and ask, is this me, is this mine? The looking is the point.
Second, Buddhist schools read it in different ways.
But notice what the sutta never says: that you don't exist.

Your body, your moods, your thoughts are all really happening. None of them is a fixed owner sitting in the middle, holding the others. There's no one piece you could point to and say, that, forever, is me.

how: Some Buddhist meditators reflect on the five aggregates, noting of each 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self', and the Anattalakkhana Sutta is among the suttas chanted in Theravada monasteries.

o: the belief that you don't really exist
giving up selfishness to serve others
no part of you is a fixed, owned self

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: the bundles that make up a person

s: the sutta never says that. it asks whether each heap is fit to be called my self.
the Buddha asks the same question about all five heaps
body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness: is it permanent, is it mine?
this was taught to the same five in the Deer Park
in the old accounts, it's the second teaching.

games.q: you're one of the five. the Buddha asks: is something impermanent fit to be called 'this is my self'? what do you say?
games.why: they answer no, five times over, and the texts say their minds were freed as they heard it.

practice: Notice whatever feeling is here right now, tiredness, worry, a little boredom, contentment, and find it in the body if you can. Then ask it gently, are you me, did I choose you, will you stay, and watch it while you ask.
There's no answer to get right; just notice what happens to a feeling when you stop assuming it's you.

wordCard.voice: Not-self. Anatta: no body, feeling, perception, habit or knowing that you can hold up and say, this, forever, is mine.

orig.note: Pali: not-self. From an- (not) and atta (self); Sanskrit anātman.

carryVoice: Your line: not mine. The feeling is real; it just isn't the owner. That's day sixty-four.
